> 「汝等勿谓如来作是念：『我当度众生。』……实无有众生如来度者。若有众生如来度者，如来即有我、人、众生、寿者。」

Section twenty-five forbids a thought — not an action, a thought — and the thought it forbids is the most virtuous one available.

Do not suppose that the Tathāgata thinks: *I shall liberate beings.*

If the Tathāgata had such a thought, the text says, he would have a self, a person, a being, a lifespan. The most compassionate sentence in the vocabulary would be evidence of the very structure the sutra has been dismantling.

## 度 without 度者

Liberation happens. Beings are confused and suffer, teaching is given, confusion ends. What does not occur is the transaction — a liberator on one side, the liberated on the other, and a deed between them that can be remembered later.

The book calls this 化无所化: transformation without a transformer. Functioning, without the two ends being occupied.

Which is not a doctrine about the Buddha's psychology. It is a description of what compassion looks like when it is not built out of a self — and the claim is that this is the only version that does not degrade.

## The mechanism, in ordinary life

Anyone who has helped someone for years knows the failure mode. The help is real, then it becomes a relationship, then a debt, then a story about who saved whom.

The story is not a side effect. It is the self being constructed out of the help — and once built, it needs the other person to remain helped, or at least grateful, in order to keep standing.

The section says: at the point where that construction starts, the help is no longer what it was.

## 如来说有我者，即非有我

Then the turn inward. The Buddha speaks of "I" — and there is no self; ordinary people take the pronoun for a person.

The distinction is grammatical and it is decisive. A word functioning as a marker of speech is not a claim that a being exists inside the speaker. The whole confusion of self, the sutra suggests, may be nothing more than a pronoun taken literally.

## 凡夫即非凡夫，是名凡夫

And the last clause extends the same treatment to the deluded: ordinary beings are not ordinary beings, therefore they are called ordinary beings.

The book's guardrail is important here, because this sentence gets used badly in two directions.

- "Everyone is already a buddha, so conduct does not matter." False: the nature being equal does not remove the difference between confusion and clarity, and confusion still hurts.
- "Ordinary beings are just a word, so their pain is not real." Also false: the pain is real at the level of conditions, which is the only level at which anyone experiences anything.

What the clause denies is a permanently deluded entity — a class of people who are, by nature, not capable. That class does not exist. It is a label applied to a moment.

## The test

Think of someone you have helped, over time. Then examine the account.

Is there gratitude you are owed? A role you occupy? A version of them that must remain worse off than you for the arrangement to hold?

None of this makes the help false. It makes it the place where the twenty-fifth section does its work.
